intro: Four classic situations you can change. Add people who give the wrong answer before you in Asch's line task, move the learner closer in Milgram's lab, change how many others can hear an emergency, and put a pool player in front of an audience. Each scene sits beside the published result from the study it is based on, with the source, and Why says what later research found.
howItWorks:
The graphs show published results only: Asch (1951, 1952, 1956), Milgram (1963, 1974), Darley and Latane (1968), Michaels and colleagues (1982) and Latane, Williams and Harkins (1979). Sizes or conditions a study did not test are not drawn. The people in the scenes are illustrations.

In Test yourself, every scenario is invented for practice and says so. First predict what happens when the situation changes, then name the concept (normative or informational influence, obedience, diffusion of responsibility, social facilitation or loafing, an attribution bias or a compliance technique), then say what later research found about the classic study.
